title: Identifying the Three Vowel Patterns of the مُضَارِع (Present Tense) Verb
summary: This session focused on identifying the middle vowel patterns for Arabic present tense (مُضَارِع) verbs. The instructor established that past tense verbs with a كَسْرَة reliably take a فَتْحَة in their present form, whereas those with a فَتْحَة are unpredictable and often require memorization or Quranic exposure. Key concepts included using الكَانَة (كَانَ) to indicate habitual past actions, the passive مَجْهُول pattern example يُقْتَلُ، and derivational vocabulary patterns like مَجْلِسٌ. The lesson concluded with a homework assignment to find three examples of each vowel type from the Quran, avoiding class-examined verbs.
key_points: The middle (third) letter of a present tense verb (مُضَارِع) can carry one of three vowels: فَتْحَة، كَسْرَة، or ضَمَّة.

A highly reliable pattern exists: if the past tense verb has a كَسْرَة on its middle letter, the corresponding مُضَارِع will take a فَتْحَة (e.g., سَمِعَ → يَسْمَعُ، فهِمَ → يَفْهَمُ، لَعِبَ → يَلْعَبُ، حَفِظَ → يَحْفِظُ). The teacher described this as taking the 'opposite' vowel position.

Past tense verbs with a فَتْحَة on their middle letter are unpredictable in the present tense; they may take a ضَمَّة، كَسْرَة، or فَتْحَة (e.g., خَرَجَ → يَخْرُجُ، فَتَحَ → يَفْتَحُ، ذَهَبَ → يَذْهَبُ). Mastery requires direct Quranic exposure or memorization.

Students familiar with the Quran (الحفّاظ) have a natural advantage because frequent recurrence of these verb forms in memorized verses causes the correct vowel to come 'on your tongue automatically,' even without knowing the exact grammatical rule.

Adding كَانَ before a مُضَارِع verb shifts its meaning to indicate a habitual or repeated action in the past (e.g., كَانُوا يَقْتُلُونَ translates to 'they used to kill on a regular basis'). Without كَانَ، it denotes regular present or future action.

The phrase كَانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا رَحِيمًا does not mean Allah was once without mercy; it translates strictly as 'Allah always was' forgiving and merciful, emphasizing pre-eternal continuity since time does not apply to Him.

The مَجْهُول (passive) voice pattern shifts the verb's form so the subject receives the action rather than performs it. Example: قُتِلَ becomes يُقْتَلُ، contextualized with the story of أَصْحَابُ الْأُخْدُودِ.

Prefixing a verb with مَ creates a derivational noun indicating a literal place of action, following the pattern of مَسْجِدٌ (place of prostration): قَعَدَ becomes مَجْلِسٌ (place of sitting), نَزَلَ becomes مَنْزِلٌ (place of staying/abode), and رَجَعَ becomes مَرْجعُ (place of return).
The instructor emphasized that identifying these vowel patterns in the Quran requires memorization for unpredictable cases, while predictable cases follow the consistent كَسْرَة-to-fathah rule.
questions: [32:58] Q: Why is the present tense verb يَقْتُلُ used in the Quran to describe a past event involving the Jews killing messengers؟ — A: It indicates a habitual past action because it follows الكَانَة (كَانَ)، meaning 'they used to do that on a regular basis.' Without الكَانَة، it simply denotes a regular present action.

[35:02] Q: Does using الكَانَة in the phrase 'كَانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا رَحِيمًا' mean Allah stopped being forgiving and merciful at some point؟ — A: No. It translates as 'Allah always was forgiving and ever-merciful.' The teacher clarified that it implies there was never a time before Him not being الْغَفُور الرَّحِيم، from pre-eternity to eternity، because time doesn't apply to Allah.

[42:30] Q: How did فَتَحَ acquire its secondary meaning of 'conquer'؟ — A: Literally، فَتَحَ means 'to open something.' It acquired the meaning of conquer because armies in that era would physically open a city's gates before entering and taking it.

quiz.q: If a past tense verb has a كَسْرَة on its middle letter، what vowel will almost always appear on that same letter in its مُضَارِع form؟
quiz.a: فتحة. The teacher explained that this is a highly reliable pattern: past tense verbs with a كَسْرَة in the middle consistently take a فَتْحَة in their مُضَارِع form (e.g., سَمِعَ becomes يَسْمَعُ).

quiz.q: When a past tense verb has a فَتْحَة on its middle letter، how many possibilities exist for the middle vowel of its مُضَارِع form؟
options: No fixed rule; it changes randomly
quiz.a: Three possibilities (فتحة، كسرة، or ضمة). The teacher noted that verbs with a فَتْحَة in the past are tricky and can take any of the three vowels in the present tense، often requiring direct Quranic exposure to know correctly.

quiz.q: What is the primary grammatical function when الكَانَة (كَانَ) is placed before a مُضَارِع verb؟
options: To indicate an action strictly in the future tense
To indicate a habitual or repeated action in the past
To change the verb into its مَجْهُول (passive) voice form
To emphasize that the action is happening right now
quiz.a: To indicate a habitual or repeated action in the past. The teacher clarified that 'كَانَ + مُضَارِع' translates to 'used to do something regularly، as seen when discussing a group that 'used to kill the messengers.'

quiz.q: How should one interpret the use of الكَانَة in Allah's attribute 'كَانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا رَحِيمًا' regarding His mercy؟
options: Allah was merciful only during a specific past period
Allah stopped being merciful before beginning again
Allah always was merciful، with no time where He was unmerciful
Mercy is applied to Allah only in the present tense
quiz.a: Allah always was merciful، with no time where He was unmerciful. The teacher stressed that this encompasses pre-eternal continuity، as 'time doesn't apply to Allah' and therefore implies never lacking mercy from eternity to eternity.

quiz.q: What is the مُضَارِع form of the مَجْهُول (passive) verb قُتِلَ mentioned in class؟
quiz.a: يُقْتَلُ. The instructor showed how قَتَلَ becomes مَجْهُول as قُتِلَ، and its corresponding present tense form shifts to يُقْتَلُ، maintaining the passive structure while explaining the context of the people of the trenches.

quiz.q: Based on the teacher's explanation of derivational nouns، what does مَجْلِسٌ literally mean؟
quiz.a: A place of sitting. The instructor explained that by adding the مَ pattern to a verb like قَعَدَ (to sit)، it forms a noun meaning 'a place of [verb action]، similar to مَسْجِدٌ.

quiz.q: Why did the instructor suggest that الحَفَّاظ have an 'edge' when learning vocabulary and verbs مثل يَخْرُجُ؟
options: They use special conjugation rules not taught in class
Frequent repetition in memorized verses naturally ingrains the forms on their tongues automatically
They rely solely on dictionary patterns for every new word
Their teachers use a completely different grading system
quiz.a: Frequent repetition in memorized verses naturally ingrains the forms on their tongues automatically. The teacher noted that while non-Huffāẓ can catch up، frequent Quranic recurrence makes the correct form come to the tongue 'not knowing why، but naturally.'

quiz.q: What specific assignment did the instructor give for homework regarding present tense verbs؟
options: Memorize the entire conjugation chart on page 71 verbatim
Identify three examples of each vowel type from the Quran، prioritizing new verbs over class examples
Write a paragraph using only past tense verbs in classical Arabic
Translate three chapters of the Quran into English grammar terms
quiz.a: Identify three examples of each vowel type from the Quran، prioritizing new verbs over class examples. The teacher initially specified five but adjusted to three after student feedback، emphasizing finding fresh verbs not already covered in session.

quiz.q: Which verb does the teacher use to demonstrate a past tense with كسرة that correctly becomes يَلْعَبُ in present tense؟
quiz.a: لَعِبَ. The instructor corrected a class example to لَعِبَ يَلْعَبُ and connected it to the story of Yūsuf، explaining that the kuffār were 'playing around' while receiving revelation.
